segments.text: Hey guys, welcome to another Flutter Mentor video.  Today, we will go over a request from last week to
explain how the Stack widget actually works.  And don't forget there are subtitles available, so
if you need them, turn them on. Now let's get to it.  Like you probably know by now, this is a simple UI.
Maybe it seems confusing, but it's really just  a container. This is the height and width. This
container right here is just the background -  the gray background - and then a Center widget, a
container that's orange, which is this whole thing.  And then there's a column with three children in
order. This is one, this is two and this is three. Green   accent is 3, pink is 2 and light blue accent is
1. Now, let's get to it. This is a Column, which is  not what we want here. We want a Stack. A Column
stacks the widgets on top of each other vertically.  But we want the Stack to overlap the widgets,
so that the widgets overlap. Like so. And maybe this  seems a little bit confusing, but the Stack widget,
as you can see, positions the first widget on the  bottom and then the following widgets on top of
each other. Here, number one - which is the blue one  if you remember - is the bottom one. Number two is
the next one. And finally number three is on top  of them. That's the usual order. Now, as it's visible
here, with Stack - without any indication - all stacks  will, by default, be positioned at the topStart,
also known as the top left corner. (depending on  text direction) But this isn't what we want. We want,
to be able to see the numbers. So, let's move it  to the bottom right corner. And to do that, we just
need to come over here to the Stack. Right here,  and use the alignment property. From here we use
AlignmentDirectional. oh, and it's the first  suggestion! bottomEnd. There we go now it looks much
better. And I'm pretty sure it's even more obvious  to you now how it works. One at the bottom, then
number two and then number three. Much like here:  Number one, number two and number three. Now, let's
say you want to give a specific child a different  positioning from the rest of the other elements.
Let's use container number three to do that. So, the  only thing you need to do is wrap said child in a
Positioned widget. And, within the Positioned widget,  you have quite a few options. And here are all of
them. These four are pretty self-explanatory once  you see the next example I'm going to show you.
And this here, actually overrides whatever the size  of the child is. But let me show you how this works.
Let me delete this one, and this one as well as  this one. Now, how does this work? First you need
to understand that, the area we're talking about  is this one and that is because the Stack's size
is inherited from its parent. The parent is the  orange container. If you come here to the top you
can see this. This orange container is the parent of the  Stack, and this right here, is the size of the Stack.
Which means that we're only concerned with this  area right here. This part is just the background
Container. So, we need to come here and input a  double. In this case, I'm gonna put 0 here and
0 here as well. And number 3 will come over  here, because we're telling Flutter that we want
this Container to have 0 distance from the left  and from the bottom. For example, if I came here to
the bottom and said 250, number 3 will show up  around here. There it is. Because now it's 250 DPIs
above the bottom. And now let's say that the left  also gets 250. Did you notice what just happened?
Container three... In fact, I'm going to make it a little  bit more obvious, and just do this. As you can tell,
Container 3 is disappearing as it goes out  of the Stack's bounds. This is normal when you use
Positioned. It's expected that a child can go out  of bounds because you're in complete control of
the position of the child. But, let's say you want  to be able to see the child outside of the Stack.
That's actually quite simple to achieve. You just  have to come here and change the overflow. Now,
the default overflow is overflow.clip, okay?  Because that's what's happening right here. It's
being clipped right as it goes beyond the bounds  of the Stack. But what we want is to see it so we
change it to "visible". And if I save this now, you  can see it go outside the bounds. Now, this isn't
the whole Container because I put it a little bit  too far to the right, but I think you got it. Now,
let me go ahead and show you how you can override  the size of the child that is being positioned.
Let's do it with the width property. As you can  see, this container has a width of 140. So, let's
give it a width of 300. And I'm not gonna save  yet, because we won't be able to see it. So, let me
give this 50. And if I save this, as you can see,  Container number 3 has massively increased
in width. And we can even make it go all the  way. Let's say left and then let's add another
50 here. And it's a perfectly fitting Container.  And now, I'm going to increase it even further...
make it 450. And let's make this negative so that  it can go over bounds on both sides. Let's say
-50, that should be enough. There you go. Now, I did  this to show you that Stack is sized by default
to fit all of its unpositioned children. And what  do I mean by this? I mean that all children of
Stack have their own width and height. But their  maximum limit is the Stack's maximum width and
height. Which, the stack inherits from its parent.  Basically, any unpositioned stacked children cannot
have a bigger size than the Stack size. And I can  show you this very easily, because this is the size
of the stack remember that this Container - with  the color deep orange - is the parent of the Stack.
So, the maximum width is 350. And, as you could see,  with the positioned child, we went overbounds. We made
it bigger than that. That's because it's positioned.  If you go over here to a non-positioned child and
make it... In fact, it's actually already bigger than  the Stack. So, this should actually have been 350,
but nothing changes. If we make it 1350, it still  remains the same. So keep that in mind when
handling with positioned and unpositioned children.  Let me go ahead and take out the width here
and make this 0 and 0. Now, something else that  can matter to you is that sometimes you might
need a child of the Stack to fill the whole Stack.  And fortunately, there is a property for that as
well. It's the fit property. Now, keep in mind that  StackFit.loose is the default property, okay?
So if I save this, nothing will change. But, if  I change it to expand, watch what happens. Boom.
Now, you may think only the second Container  changed, but if I come here and I change it to
a positioned child - and let's just, I don't know,  let's give it and put it on the right - and if
we save this... you can see the blue also expanded.  And attention, if this this was just a positioned
widget and you didn't define anything for it,  it still expands. Because, technically this is
not a positioned child. Because, the widget is  not actually doing anything. It's pointless.
So, Flutter (very intelligently) ignores it.  Now, lastly, (let me just remove this here)
what happens if the Stack has no parent? Then  the Stack turns to its children and sees what the
biggest one is and let's give this one 550 width.  And then on the height, let's make... let's make this
one here the tallest one give it a 300. Now if we  save this, obviously the orange disappears. And now
this, from here to here, is the stack size. In fact,  if I come over here you'll understand better. As
you can see, this blue line... this is the whole  Stack size. And something also very interesting
is that if I come over here again and I do 250...  Do you think that the Stack size increased or not?
Pause the video and think about it. Okay, it didn't.  Because, as you can see, the blue line is still
here. Now, what happened was we positioned one of  the children 250 DPIs above the bottom here. But
the Stack size is still the same. The only thing  that's happening is that the positioned child is out
of bounds. In fact, if you remember how to clip it,  if you come here and change this to clip and save...
Boom, it's now being clipped and here you  can really tell exactly what the Stack
size is. I truly hope this video has helped you  better understand how Stack works in general.
And, if you did learn something, I would be  so grateful if you could like this video and
subscribe... that would really support this channel  and give me motivation to keep on creating
these videos for you guys. So, without anything  further to add, this is Flutter Mentor... aaaand OUT.
